title: What Happens to Your Achilles tendon If You do calf raises on the stairs Every Day
description: Calf raises on a stair edge are the full-range version of the strongest tendon habit there is. Here is what doing them every day does to your Achilles over four weeks, and the calf test that grades your spring honestly.

scenes.narration: Stand on one foot on the edge of a step, heel hanging off, hand lightly on the rail. Rise to your highest point, then lower until your heel drops below the step. That full journey is one rep. Count clean reps until you cannot reach the top. That number is your Achilles grade. Test both feet and write down the weaker side. The stair version is stricter than the floor, and the difference between the two tests is the story of this episode.

scenes.label: THE FULL-RANGE LINE
scenes.sub: under 8 on stairs: tendon untrained - over 20: achilles is wired
scenes.narration: Here is the line for the stair test. Under eight full-range reps, your Achilles is untrained in the deep range, which is where springs are made. Eight to fifteen is the build zone. Over twenty slow reps per side on a step edge means your Achilles is a heavy-duty cable, and your running, jumping and climbing all know it.

Week one is a range discovery. On the floor, your calf raise ends where the ground says so. On the stair, your heel travels below the start, and the Achilles gets loaded through a stretch it rarely feels in daily life. The first days feel awkward and deep, and the weaker ankle wobbles at the bottom. That wobble is information: the bottom of the range is exactly where your spring has been sleeping.

beats.title: LOADED IN THE STRETCH
lines: The bottom is where springs sleep.

scenes.narration: Week two is the remodeling shift. Lowering slowly into that deep stretch is called eccentric loading, and it is the most studied tendon stimulus in sports science: the exact signal that tells tendon tissue to add collagen and reorganize its fibers. Your daily stair set delivers it perfectly, rep after rep, with nothing but your bodyweight and a step. The reps get slower and prouder. Slow is not weakness here. Slow is the construction speed of tendon.

By week four your spring has been rebuilt at full length. A tendon trained through its whole range is stiff where it should be and supple where it must be, returning energy from positions the floor version never reaches. That is why stair-trained calves show up everywhere: the first step of a sprint, the top of a climb, the landing of a jump. For a skinny guy this is the purest free upgrade in the body, one step edge away. If your Achilles is ever sore and stiff every morning for a week, back off and see a professional if it persists.
Now raise with me on the edge. Up tall, lower below the step, slow both ways. Thirty seconds a side. Go.

The protocol is a daily stair set per side. Rise for two seconds, pause at the top, lower for three seconds into the full stretch. Train the weaker side first and match it on the strong side. Keep your knee straight and your hips level, and hold the rail for balance only, never to pull yourself up. When twenty clean reps feel easy, slow the lowering to five seconds before you add any weight. The step edge is a complete gym for this tendon.

Your stair number, judged. Under eight: the deep range is asleep, and the month ahead wakes it rep by rep. Eight to fifteen: the build zone, where week three usually evens the sides and doubles control. Over twenty per side: a wired Achilles, so chase the five-second lowering. Retest on day twenty-eight on the same step and comment your new number. Just the number.

One step edge, one set a day, and the strongest tendon you own gets rebuilt at full length. Start tomorrow, lower slow, and let your spring come back stronger every week. Subscribe for the next daily test. This is {channel}. Train the cable.
